“It is not the number of years you have spent in life, but how much
life you have given to those years.” — Prof. Sivakumar
What is a growth mindset?

blocks.html: The idea comes from the psychologist Carol Dweck. She studied what makes people perform at their best.
blocks.text:
The idea comes from the psychologist Carol Dweck .
She studied what makes people perform at their best.

blocks.html: People who believe their talents can be developed (through hard work, good strategies and input from others) have a growth mindset. People who believe their talents are fixed (inborn gifts) have a fixed mindset. (Based on Dweck’s article “What Having a ‘Growth Mindset’ Actually Means”, Harvard Business Review.)
blocks.text:
People who believe their talents can be developed (through hard work, good strategies and input from others) have a growth mindset . People who believe their talents are fixed (inborn gifts) have a fixed
mindset . (Based on Dweck’s article “What Having a ‘Growth
Mindset’ Actually Means”, Harvard Business Review.)

blocks.html: People with a growth mindset achieve more. They worry less about looking smart and put more energy into learning. In companies with a growth mindset, employees feel more empowered and committed, and there is more support for teamwork and new ideas.
blocks.text:
People with a growth mindset achieve more . They
worry less about looking smart and put more energy into learning . In companies with a growth mindset, employees
feel more empowered and committed , and
there is more support for teamwork and new ideas.

Fixed vs growth: five
differences

blocks.caption:
The same situations, seen through
two different mindsets.

blocks.html:
Situation ✗ Fixed mindset ✓ Growth mindset
Challenges Avoids them Embraces them
Setbacks Gives up early Keeps going
Effort Sees it as useless Sees it as the path to mastery
Criticism Ignores useful feedback; takes it personally Learns from it
Others’ success Feels threatened or jealous Finds lessons and inspiration in it
blocks.text: Situation ✗ Fixed mindset ✓ Growth mindset Challenges Avoids them Embraces them Setbacks Gives up early Keeps going Effort Sees it as useless Sees it as the path to mastery Criticism Ignores useful feedback; takes it personally Learns from it Others’ success Feels threatened or jealous Finds lessons and inspiration in it
Three personal stories

blocks.html:
Lecture example — Prof. Kartic: “I had to be the best in everything” Early in life, he avoided challenges, gave up easily, and wanted to look smart. He took criticism as an attack on himself, not on his work, so it made him angry and frustrated. He couldn’t stand others doing better. This took a toll on his mental and physical health. With mentors and self-reflection, he changed:

  • Performance is about the process, not just results.
  • Learn from setbacks.
  • Success is the path to mastery, not winning every time.
  • Criticism is about the task, not the person.
  • Get inspired by others’ success, not threatened.
blocks.text:

everything” Early in life, he avoided challenges, gave up
easily, and wanted to look smart. He took criticism as an attack on himself , not on his work , so it
made him angry and frustrated. He couldn’t stand others doing better.
This took a toll on his mental and physical health. With mentors and
self-reflection, he changed: Performance is about the process , not just
results. Learn from setbacks. Success is the path to mastery , not winning every

threatened.

blocks.html: Lecture example — Prof. Prasanna: the “brain freeze” After a top rank, she came to IIT Madras and felt clueless and out of place. She built a comfort zone, avoided challenges, and told herself, “If I can’t do it right the first time, I can’t do it at all”, and “Engineering is not for me.” One day she realised that staying in her comfort zone, ruled by fears and excuses, had given her nothing. That was her “moment of truth”. She saw that her happiness was her responsibility and that she had the power of choice. She started exploring, experimenting and making mistakes. She turned stumbling blocks into stepping stones and used words of power and positivity.

Words change your mindset

blocks.html: Prof. Sivakumar noticed that small word changes shift thinking:
blocks.text: Prof. Sivakumar noticed that small word changes shift thinking:

blocks.caption:
Small changes in words create a big change in
mindset.

blocks.html:
Instead of… Say… Why it helps
“Let’s divide the 10 people into two teams.” “Let’s group them into two teams.” Grouping brings people together; dividing splits them.
“What is your course load next semester?” “I am offering a course next semester.” “Offering” feels like giving, not a burden.
Being jealous of someone’s success Appreciating their success To appreciate means to increase the value of something. When you appreciate others, you learn how they succeeded, and you grow too.

sections.title: Four Zones of Growth and Handling Rejection

blocks.html: Start here A first-year student joined every club and competition, won none, and wrote, “My life is a failure. I don’t belong at IIT.” Two years later he was nearly the topper and won a hockey silver. A simple juggling game changed his thinking.
blocks.text:
Start here A first-year student joined every club
and competition, won none, and wrote, “My life is a failure. I don’t
belong at IIT.” Two years later he was nearly the topper and won a
hockey silver. A simple juggling game changed his thinking.
The four zones of growth

blocks.html: When you try something new, you move through four zones:
blocks.text:
When you try something new, you move through four
zones :

blocks.caption:
From the comfort zone, through fear
and learning, to growth.

blocks.html:
Zone How it feels
1. Comfort zone You feel safe and in control. Nothing new happens here.
2. Fear zone You lack self-confidence. You make excuses and worry about what others think.
3. Learning zone You face challenges and solve problems. You learn new skills, and your comfort zone grows bigger.
4. Growth zone You find your purpose, set new goals and achieve them.

blocks.html: Lecture example — the juggling pencils Prof. Sivakumar, then a guidance and counselling adviser, invited the student to his office. He threw pencils to him one after another: “Catch this, catch this, catch this…” When the student missed one, he panicked and missed the next, and the next: a downward spiral. That was exactly what had happened in his IIT life: failure in one activity spread into failure in the others. The tip: “If you miss one, it’s okay. Just focus on the next.” The student started catching more. His lesson: “I should not join everything. I will pick and choose.” Two years later, he wrote to say he was nearly the topper in his branch and had won a silver in hockey.

Missing one catch doesn’t mean
you’ll miss them all. Focus on the next one.

blocks.html: Lesson: When you don’t feel safe or in control, you can’t learn. Choose a few things, focus, and don’t let one failure spread into everything.

Handling rejection

blocks.html: Rejection happens to everyone: in interviews, promotions, project proposals, business deals and personal life.
blocks.text:
Rejection happens to everyone: in interviews, promotions, project
proposals, business deals and personal life.

blocks.html:
Type of rejection What it looks like
External Someone says “No”
Internal Your own limiting beliefs, fears and negative self-talk
blocks.text:
Type of rejection What it looks like External Someone says “No” Internal Your own limiting beliefs, fears and negative
self-talk

blocks.html: “If you are trying to avoid failure, you have already failed, because you are not even trying.” — Prof. Kartic, summing up J. K. Rowling’s famous Harvard speech
blocks.text:
“If you are trying to avoid failure, you have already failed, because

blocks.html: Goal: turn resistance into persistence.
blocks.text:
Goal: turn resistance into
persistence .

blocks.html: Lecture example — Prof. Kartic: the missing simulation games A client wanted simulation games. He offered only board, card and some digital games, so the deal didn’t happen. Instead of giving up, he asked himself, “Why am I limiting myself?” He found partners who made simulation games. Six to eight months later, he contacted the same client, who still hadn’t found a supplier. The talks restarted. The deal finally failed because of the client’s budget, but he was happy. He had changed his mindset from “I must provide everything” to “I am part of an ecosystem that solves the client’s problem.”

blocks.html: Lecture example — Prof. Sivakumar: “Did you ask why he said no?” Students needed an electric vehicle for a solar-vehicle competition. They were too shy to ask the Dean of Students’ office. When they finally asked, the answer was no, and they came back. He sent them back to ask: “Why?” Understanding the reason behind a “no” helps you pitch better next time. They finally found a vehicle elsewhere. Lesson: there will be rejection and resistance. Persist, understand the “no”, and grow.

The upside-down drawing
activity

blocks.html: Three students copied a drawing in two ways:
blocks.text: Three students copied a drawing in two ways:

blocks.html:
1. The normal way: look at the picture and copy it.
  2. Upside down: turn the picture upside down and cover most of it, so only a small strip shows. Copy that strip, then move down.
blocks.text:
The normal way: look at the picture and copy
it. Upside down: turn the picture upside down and cover
most of it, so only a small strip shows. Copy that strip, then move
down.

blocks.caption:
Upside down, your brain stops
saying “this must look like a horse” and just draws lines.

blocks.html:
Student What they said
Tushar (said he “can’t draw”) First try: worried it looked like a donkey and kept “fixing” it. Second try: noticed more details and felt more peaceful.
Anamika (good at drawing) Upside down felt strange, just lines and wiggles. She expected it to go wrong, trusted the process, and it came out fine. “Doing something unconventional won’t always lead to a bad result.”
Anirudha (doesn’t feel creative) The second try was less stressful, because he saw lines, not “a horse that must be perfect”. He gained confidence that with practice and the right method, he can improve.

Words are powerful

blocks.html: Ending negative self-talk clears your mind and opens up creativity. Words create, so use words of power and positivity in the present to create the future you want.

blocks.html: Prof. Prasanna also refers to a video by Jim Kwik on how to stop negative self-talk: acknowledge the chatter, don’t fight it, let it go, and then align with your goals using positive words and actions.

The ABRA method

blocks.html:
Step What to do
A — Acknowledge Notice the chatter. Don’t fight your limitations or argue with them. What you resist, persists.
B — Breathe Breathe in what you want.
R — Release Let go of what you don’t want: release your limitations.
A — Align Align with who you are, who you wish to become, and the future you wish to create.

blocks.html: Lecture example — the conference checklist In 2005, Prof. Sivakumar had to organise a big conference: about 300 participants, many from abroad, to be opened by President A. P. J. Abdul Kalam. He was very tense. A colleague sat him down for 15 minutes and listed every task, with who would do it. Seeing the full list, his tension vanished. The event ran “like clockwork”. Lesson: Worry grows in your head. Writing a clear list turns it into steps.

sections.title: The Benefits of Failure and the Mouse Merchant

blocks.html: Start here A research student runs in: “Sir, the experiment didn’t work!” The professor smiles: “Good! Now you have a question to ask — why didn’t it work?” Failure is just information.
blocks.text:
Start here A research student runs in: “Sir, the
experiment didn’t work!” The professor smiles: “Good! Now you have a

Failure is a stepping stone

blocks.caption:
Each “failed” attempt is one
step closer.

blocks.html:
Example The reframe
Research scholars “It didn’t work” becomes “Now I can ask why.” Failure gives you many questions, and questions lead to research.
Thomas Edison Asked how he kept going after so many failures, he reportedly said he never failed; each attempt showed one more material that won’t work. Thinking this way helped him develop a practical light bulb.
Glass half full or half empty The same event can be seen as a failure or as new understanding. Life isn’t an exam.

blocks.html: Prof. Prasanna’s points:

blocks.html:
• Knowing what can go wrong while making a crispy dosa is as useful as knowing how to make it. The best recipe blogs list common mistakes and fixes.
  • Software or a product is only as strong as its exception handling. Testers look for failure points (unit, integration, system, acceptance and stress testing) so they can be fixed.

J. K. Rowling:
“The Fringe Benefits of Failure”

blocks.html: This lecture is named after J. K. Rowling’s famous Harvard speech (2008), “The Fringe Benefits of Failure, and the Importance of Imagination”. Her main ideas:
blocks.text:
This lecture is named after J. K. Rowling’s famous Harvard speech (2008) , “The Fringe Benefits of Failure,
and the Importance of Imagination”. Her main ideas:

blocks.html:
• It is impossible to live without failing at something, unless you live so carefully that you hardly live at all. And that is a failure too.
  • Failure strips away what is not essential, so you can focus on what matters.
  • Imagination lets us dream up a better future, and also lets us empathise with others.
blocks.text:
It is impossible to live without failing at
something, unless you live so carefully that you hardly live at all. And
that is a failure too. Failure strips away what is not essential , so you
can focus on what matters. Imagination lets us dream up a better future, and
also lets us empathise with others.
The Mouse Merchant story

blocks.html: This is an old Indian tale (from the Jataka tales): how a poor young man became rich by making the most of whatever he had.
blocks.text:
This is an old Indian tale (from the Jataka tales ):
how a poor young man became rich by making the most of whatever
he had .

blocks.caption:
From one dead mouse to a fortune, one
small step at a time.

blocks.html: The story in short:
blocks.text: The story in short:

blocks.html:
1. A poor young man hears a wise man say that a smart person could build a fortune even from a dead mouse on the road.
  2. He picks it up and sells it to a shopkeeper as food for a cat, earning one small coin.
  3. With the coin he buys jaggery and offers jaggery and water to tired flower-pickers. They thank him with flowers, which he sells.
  4. A storm wrecks a garden and leaves branches everywhere. He offers to clear it for free if he may keep the wood, then sells the wood.
  5. He keeps spotting chances like these (for example, helping grass-cutters, then using their grass when a horse dealer comes to town), and step by step he becomes a rich merchant.
blocks.text:
A poor young man hears a wise man say that a smart person could
build a fortune even from a dead mouse on the
road. He picks it up and sells it to a shopkeeper as food for a
cat , earning one small coin. With the coin he buys jaggery and offers jaggery
and water to tired flower-pickers . They thank him with flowers , which he sells. A storm wrecks a garden and leaves branches
everywhere. He offers to clear it for free if he may
keep the wood , then sells the wood. He keeps spotting chances like these (for example, helping
grass-cutters, then using their grass when a horse dealer comes to
town), and step by step he becomes a rich
merchant .

blocks.html: What the students and teachers took from it:
blocks.text: What the students and teachers took from it:

blocks.html:
• “Where there is a will, there is a way.” (Anamika)
  • Look at the positive side. If you only complain about misfortune, you stay stuck. Misfortune is temporary. (Anamika)
  • Persistence and confidence: he must have faced failures too, but he kept going and grabbed opportunities. (Aniruddha)
  • Spot hidden opportunities: the storm-damaged garden looked like a problem, but the wood was an opportunity. (Prof. Sivakumar)

sections.title: Positive and Abundance Mindset — and the Growth Mindset Card Game

blocks.html: Start here Is the glass half full or half empty? Look again: the other half is full of air, and above that is endless space. If you see the whole picture, the glass is infinitely full. So is your potential.

Lack vs abundance

blocks.html:
Lack mindset Abundance mindset
“I don’t have enough.” “I have all the resources I need to take the next step.”
Sees only what’s missing Lists everything available, and finds many ways forward

blocks.html: Prof. Prasanna’s line, inspired by the Mouse Merchant: “You have all the resources you need at any instant of time to take the next step or action in your life.”
blocks.text:
Prof. Prasanna’s line, inspired by the Mouse Merchant: “You have all the resources you need at any instant of time
to take the next step or action in your life.”

Five ways to build an
abundance mindset

blocks.caption:
Curiosity, power words,
gratitude, resourcefulness and giving.

blocks.html:
# Habit What it means
1 Be open and curious About life and growth. Good or bad, ask what you can learn from it.
2 Use words of power and positivity Focus on what you want (healthy, happy, productive, creative, helpful), not on what went wrong. What you think and imagine tends to become real.
3 Practise gratitude, and journal it The opposite of gratitude is entitlement: thinking we deserve everything. We take so much for granted: family, teachers, support staff, even this video shoot. Write it down; on hard days, your journal reminds you of the good.
4 Be resourceful Use all your resources. Internal (intangible): strengths, talents, gifts, habits, values, beliefs, potential. External (tangible): money, time, people, natural and man-made resources. Remember your “moments of greatness” and what helped you then.
5 Give back Share generously to make a difference. Many people helped us without expecting anything back. Repay by paying it forward: take from the universe in one form, give back to the universe in another.

blocks.html: Lecture example — the cycle lamp At the military academy, cadets had to use a bicycle lamp after dark. One cadet rode without it: “Sir, there’s light all around — streetlights, moonlight!” The instructor let the air out of both his tyres: “There’s air all around. Keep going!” Lesson: abundance is real, but for professional growth, still follow the rules.

The Growth Mindset Card Game

blocks.html: The faculty played a game based on UNO. You match a card’s colour or number to discard it, and the first player with no cards wins. Some cards have a statement you must respond to:

player with no cards wins. Some cards have a statement you must respond to:

blocks.html:

  • True or false.
  • Fixed or growth?
  • Fill in the blank.

blocks.caption:
Turn fixed-mindset words into
growth-mindset words.

blocks.text: Reframes from the game

blocks.html:
Fixed-mindset statement Growth-mindset reframe
“I always get in trouble.” “I do get into trouble, but each time I learn to handle it better.”
“I always mess things up.” “I make mistakes, but I learn from them.” (Prof. Kartic now organises his folders and tax planning better.)
“I’m terrible at organising.” “I’m not good at organising yet, but I can improve with practice.” (He went from leading 20 people to 300–400.)
“I won’t try out for the play; I’ll forget my lines.” “That’s exactly why I should try. I’ll improve, and the prompters will help.”
“I’ll never have any friends.” The word “never” shows a fixed mindset. Reframe: “I will find friends by talking to people and listening.”
“I’m not going to play the game because I always lose.” “If I lose 10 times, I learn, and maybe I win the 11th.” Losing is learning.

True or false? (the
faculty’s answers)

blocks.html:
Statement Answer
Your brain grows, changes and gets smarter the more you challenge yourself. True
Some people are just born lucky and get everything right the first time. False: the practice and persistence behind success are often hidden.
It is not always easy to have a growth mindset. The Colonel said false: it is a matter of your own thinking. People at the top climbed step by step while others slept.
Ignoring a problem will make it go away. False: Prof. Sivakumar avoided public talks, and the next invitation just came along.
You believe you can do hard things. True: ask “What can I do? What will I learn? What’s the first step?”
“I’m afraid I might mess up, but I’m going to try anyway.” Growth mindset
“I can do tough things.” Growth mindset: the Colonel’s commando course built up from 10 km to a 40 km speed march carrying 30–35 kg.

Gift What it does
Mind The creative space where you think, feel, imagine and plan
Body A “super smart device” that turns your thoughts into words and actions, and feeds back what you experience
Brain Links mind and body. What you put in your mind is like a program: the brain turns it into actions and results.

The 4R framework
1. ReCHARGE your mind and body

blocks.html: When a problem hits, your energy drops. You worry, panic, overthink. So first, step back and recharge.

blocks.html: Ways to recharge: meditation, emotional cleansing, journaling, gratitude, good food, sleep, exercise, breathwork, talking to someone, hobbies (books, movies, music, sports), and time in nature (the beach, a long drive, trekking).

2. ReSOURCE your potential

blocks.html: In a crisis, we forget everything we have achieved. Self-doubt creeps in. So remember your personal capital:
blocks.text:

blocks.html:
Expressed potential = personal capital Potential yet to be shown
Core values; strengths, talents, abilities, skills, habits; purpose, vision, mission; successes and achievements; lessons and insights; connections Your goals, aspirations, dreams and the impact you want to make
Remembering what you’ve already overcome boosts your morale.
blocks.text: Remembering what you’ve already overcome boosts your morale .

3. ReVIEW and ReFRAME your
strategy

blocks.html: Ask yourself:
blocks.text: Ask yourself:

blocks.html:
• Mindset and beliefs: what shift do I need: fixed → growth, lack → abundance, negative → positive?
  • Words: which words fit the future I want?
  • Intentions and expectations: which ones do I need to rethink?
  • Possibilities and choices: what else could I try?
  • Behaviours and habits: what needs an upgrade?
  • Short term vs long term: instant gratification, or long-term benefit?
  • Impact on others: how does this affect people close to me? Does it make the world better?
  • Resources: what can I do myself (insource), and who or what can help (outsource: people, money, materials)?

blocks.text: Fixed vs growth (Carol Dweck)

blocks.html:
Fixed Growth
Avoids challenges Embraces challenges
Gives up early Persists through setbacks
Effort is useless Effort is the path to mastery
Ignores criticism Learns from criticism
Threatened by others’ success Inspired by others’ success

Zones and rejection

blocks.html:
• Four zones: comfort (safe, in control) → fear (no confidence, excuses) → learning (face challenges, new skills) → growth (purpose, new goals).
  • Juggling pencils: miss one, focus on the next. Don’t do everything at once.
  • Rejection: external (“no”) and internal (limiting beliefs, fear, self-talk). Turn resistance into persistence.
  • Ask why the answer was no (solar vehicle). Become part of an ecosystem (simulation-game partners). “The answer is yes” (army logistics).

End negative self-talk

blocks.html:
• Upside-down drawing (Betty Edwards): no judgment means less stress and more detail.
  • ABRA: Acknowledge (don’t fight; what you resist persists) → Breathe in what you want → Release what you don’t want → Align with who you want to be.
  • Process over result (Dhoni). Write the list (the 2005 conference opened by Kalam).

Failure and the Mouse
Merchant

blocks.html:
• Failure = a stepping stone and a source of questions (research scholars, Edison).
  • Knowing what can go wrong = exception handling. Cake → pudding. Grade down from 100.
  • J. K. Rowling’s Harvard speech: failure strips away the inessential; imagination builds the future and empathy.
  • Mouse Merchant (Jataka tale): dead mouse → coin → jaggery and water → flowers → wood from a storm-hit garden → fortune. Make the most of what you have; spot hidden opportunities.
  • COVID: online work saved travel and reached the world.

Abundance mindset

blocks.html:
• Half full? With air and space, the glass is infinitely full.
  • Five habits: be open and curious; use words of power; gratitude journal (the opposite is entitlement); be resourceful (internal and external); give back / pay it forward.
  • Card game (UNO-style): reframe “I always lose”, “I’ll never have friends” (the word never), “I’m terrible at organising” (add yet).

The 4R framework

blocks.html:
1. Recharge mind and body (meditation, sleep, nature…).
  2. Resource your potential (personal capital).
  3. Review and Reframe your strategy (mindset, words, habits, resources).
  4. Refocus to take inspired action (tiny steps, tiny gains).
